limitations: Retrospective series of 22 adolescents reported almost entirely as cohort statistics; roster of individuals is incomplete. Only six patients are individually identifiable (Table 1 footnote, patient I/II/III paranoid schizophrenia, I/II catatonic schizophrenia, one schizoaffective), and the other sixteen are not enumerated.

Cohort means, percentages, response rates (82%), PANSS scores, adverse-event counts, ECT parameters (sessions, intensity, seizure duration), EEG/imaging/laboratory findings and medication counts are not assigned to any individual patient.

Cohort-wide statements ("All patients"/"Every patient": >=2 antipsychotic trials, >=14 days of medication before ECT, antagonist drug classes, ECT protocol and anesthesia, full-course completion, no serious adverse events, ward setting) are not converted into facts for the six footnote patients; each patient keeps only footnote-specific data plus the study-population ICD-10 diagnosis; the cohort age definition (adolescents, analysis up to age 19) is not copied to individuals.

Source inconsistencies kept unresolved at cohort level: ECT sessions "ranged from 10 to 12 (mean: 12.4)" (mean exceeds maximum); "In ten patients, at least one ineffective seizure was recorded" vs 4+3+1 = 8 patients in the breakdown; EEG abnormalities "81.4% of patients (N = 18)" whereas 18/22 = 81.8%. Methods give weight-based propofol/succinylcholine doses without atropine whereas Results give absolute mg ranges with atropine and etomidate in one patient (not a numerical contradiction).

Conclusions state ECT is effective for adolescents "with both psychotic and mood disorders", but the Discussion notes a lack of mood disorder patients and the cohort included only schizophrenia/schizoaffective diagnoses; cohort-level only.
No dates, durations of hospitalization or follow-up for individuals; the abstract/discussion state lack of long-term follow-up.
